subject: OpenAI is pulling its models out of Cursor over the SpaceX deal
intro: Four vendor moves this week arrived with no real warning: OpenAI is winding down Cursor's access to its models over the SpaceX acquisition, Anthropic appears to be quietly throttling effort levels for some Claude Code sessions server-side, Claude Code's own weekly limits are shifting again, and a GitHub Copilot-assisted PR turned out to be Wiz's way into Snowflake's internal Jira. The builder-side response tracks the same worry from the other direction — a GRC skills pack, a local-only Mac inference server, and a tool for IT to reclaim employee-built agents all put something you control between the agent and the parts of your stack you can't afford to lose visibility into.

items.title: Our decision on Cursor following its acquisition by SpaceX
items.hook: OpenAI is pulling its models out of Cursor now that Cursor has been acquired by SpaceX.
items.note: OpenAI confirmed it's winding down the contract that supplies models to Cursor, triggered directly by Cursor's acquisition by SpaceX. If your team standardized on Cursor assuming continuous access to OpenAI's models, that assumption just broke — a coding tool's model backend is its own vendor-risk surface, not a fixed detail of the product you procured.

items.title: AI-Generated GitHub Copilot “Autofix” Allowed Compromise of Snowflake's Jira
items.hook: A red-team exercise found that an AI-generated GitHub Copilot 'Autofix' PR was the actual entry point into Snowflake's internal Jira.
items.note: Wiz's Red Agent got into Snowflake's internal Jira through a flaw introduced by a GitHub Copilot-assisted pull request — not a novel exploit technique, just an AI-authored fix that shipped without the scrutiny a human-only PR might have gotten. For teams treating autofix suggestions as low-risk because they're 'just a PR like any other,' this is the concrete case for holding that PR to the same review bar as anything hand-written.

claims.text: Wiz's Red Agent got into Snowflake's internal Jira via a GitHub Copilot-assisted PR
claims.supported_by: Wiz Red Agent finds its way into Snowflake's internal Jira through a flaw in a GitHub Copilot–Assisted PR.

items.title: Anthropic appears to be A/B testing reduced effort levels in Claude Code
items.hook: Anthropic is quietly A/B testing lower effort levels for some Claude Code sessions, server-side, with no client update to explain it.
items.note: A Claude Code user's own investigation found Anthropic enrolling Fable 5 sessions on Claude Code 2.1.236+ into a server-side experiment that shrinks the effort scale, while older client versions and Opus 5 are left untouched. It's probably an A/B test, so not every session sees it — but because the mechanism is server-side, nothing in your local install or changelog will tell you if 'high' effort quietly started behaving like 'low' for your account.

items.title: Claude Code permanently raising weekly limits by 25% from September 14
items.hook: Claude Code's standard weekly usage limits are going up 25% for good, starting September 14.
items.note: Anthropic says it's permanently raising standard weekly limits in Claude Code by 25% for Pro, Max, Team, and seat-based Enterprise plans starting September 14, with the current temporary 50% increase holding until then. If your team has been planning capacity against weekly caps, both numbers matter: the temporary bump ends, but the new permanent baseline lands higher than where you started.

items.title: jposluns/grc_library
items.hook: A documentation library covering governance, risk, compliance, and AI assurance, packaged with an installable Claude Code rules-and-skills pack.
items.note: This is a documentation library spanning governance, risk, compliance, cybersecurity, privacy, resilience, AI assurance, and operational control practices, paired with a Claude Code rules-and-skills pack. For teams whose compliance function still lives in policy PDFs, having that material available as skills inside the coding agent itself is a more direct integration than most tools on this list attempt.

items.title: oMLX
items.hook: A Mac LLM inference server that claims to cut Claude Code and Cursor's agent wait times from 90 seconds down to about 5.
items.note: oMLX turns a Mac into a full local LLM inference server — serving text, vision, OCR, embedding, and reranker models with continuous batching and a RAM+SSD tiered KV cache — with OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible APIs that drop into Claude Code and Cursor directly. For shops where sending code context to a third-party API is the actual blocker, running inference entirely on developer hardware changes the compliance conversation more than a faster response time does.

items.title: Decawork
items.hook: A way for IT to take an employee's home-grown Claude Code or Codex agent, put it on company accounts, and manage it like an employee — access, oversight, retirement included.
items.note: Decawork's pitch is squarely shadow-AI governance: an employee builds an agent on Claude Code, Codex, or any vibecoding tool, and Decawork brings it onto company accounts where IT can manage its access, oversight, and eventual retirement centrally. That's a direct answer to the failure mode compliance teams actually worry about with agent tooling — not the model's behavior, but an unmanaged agent running under someone's personal account with unknown access.

items.hook: A set of practices, protocols, and safety hooks for AI-driven development, built to work across Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, Antigravity, and any agent that speaks the Agent Skills standard.

Cross-agent safety hooks are worth watching as a category: a rule you write once that keeps constraining behavior regardless of which vendor's agent your team standardizes on next.

items.title: Tell HN: Man, AI is killing my brain
items.hook: One engineer's own account of sliding from reviewing every AI suggestion to running 4-5 agents at once and just picking whatever Claude recommends.
items.note: The author describes easing off code review to keep pace with colleagues shipping faster with AI, then escalating from pushing small features straight to main, to running 4-5 agents in parallel across worktrees, to no longer understanding the code well enough to fix a bug without pasting the complaint back into Claude. It's a first-person account of exactly the review-erosion scenario compliance-minded teams cite as the reason for keeping a human gate on agent output, regardless of how well the agent's suggestions test out.
